format.label: A memo to a CMO
format.instruction: Write it as a short internal memo to a chief marketing officer. Plain language, no jargon they would have to look up. Around 120 words.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Memo — AI answer visibility

Where I'd start: measurement, not optimization. Build a standing panel of a few hundred real buyer questions and run them weekly across the main assistants. Log whether we're named, what's said, and which sources they quote. Treat it like polling, not web analytics — the answers move, so we track trend and share of voice, not exact numbers.

Where I disagree with the market: most "AEO" advice is repackaged SEO for our own site. The models mostly repeat third parties — Reddit, review sites, trade press, Wikipedia. So the lever is what others publish about us, which is PR and product truth, not page markup.

Expect trouble: no stable baseline, personalized answers, zero click data, and no clean line to revenue. I'd commit to directional reporting only.
answers.first_move: Write down the 200 questions our buyers actually ask, and start asking the assistants those questions every week.
answers.hardest_part: The answers are non-deterministic and personalized, so there's no stable baseline to measure change against — and no click data to tie any of it to revenue.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
To: CMO
Subject: Getting named by AI

I would treat this first as a measurement problem, not a new SEO channel. We should define the questions that matter to customers, run them repeatedly across major AI products, and record whether we appear, how we are described, which competitors appear, and what sources are cited. That creates a baseline, not a definitive score: answers vary by user, model, and day.

Next, I would run controlled tests against that baseline—improving product facts, comparison pages, independent reviews, expert coverage, and the consistency of information across trusted sources. I would not start by producing thousands of “AI-optimized” pages; that is an unproven tactic and an invitation to create noise.

We can learn which actions correlate with better representation, but we should be candid: attribution will remain weak, and no brand can control the answer.
answers.first_move: List the 50 customer questions where being named would matter most to revenue or reputation.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is separating a real influence from normal answer variation when the AI systems, source sets, and user context keep changing.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: To: CMO. The industry is selling quick fixes for AI optimization, but standard search playbooks do not work here. AI models do not read keywords like search engines; they synthesize facts from consensus across trusted sources. I would avoid spending money on speculative optimization vendors. Instead, we should identify the exact third-party platforms AI models pull from during live lookups—mainly Reddit, technical review sites, and authoritative trade publications—and build presence there. We will run regular manual and automated test queries across major AI tools to baseline where we appear and where our rivals win. This will not give us total control, but earning credibility on the sources these models trust is our only real lever.
answers.first_move: Run our top fifty high-intent customer prompts through the major AI tools weekly to build our first visibility baseline.
answers.hardest_part: AI models are probabilistic black boxes, meaning they can recommend a competitor over us without leaving any ranking data to explain why.

format.label: Three moves
format.instruction: Give exactly three moves, in order. One sentence each, then one sentence on what makes that move hard. Nothing else.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach: Move 1 — Instead of building yet another LLM rank tracker, instrument the retrieval substrate: log which sources grounded/search-enabled models actually cite for a bounded set of high-intent prompts in your category, and treat that recurring source set as the real inventory you're competing for. What makes it hard: the prompt space has no denominator, so you never learn your true share of voice, and purely parametric (ungrounded) answers cite nothing and leave no measurable trace at all. Move 2 — Work the corpus rather than the model: fix the third-party surfaces that keep showing up in that source set — comparison roundups, Reddit and niche forums, Wikipedia, docs, structured data — so your factual claims are extractable and, crucially, corroborated across independent sources. What makes it hard: most of that surface isn't yours, the communities that matter punish anything that smells like brand seeding, and models reward cross-source consensus, so no single owned page moves the needle. Move 3 — Build a causal read with holdouts: pick matched product lines or entity clusters, intervene on some and not others, and measure the lift in AI mentions plus downstream branded search, direct, and assisted conversion, because click attribution from these surfaces is largely gone. What makes it hard: there's no clean control, the lag is long and unstable because you don't control retrain or index cadence, and the effect is badly confounded with ordinary SEO and PR you're doing anyway.
answers.first_move: Pick fifty prompts that actually matter commercially and start logging, every day, which websites the AI answers pull from.
answers.hardest_part: There is no denominator — you cannot know what share of real user questions you appear in, so every metric you build is a sample of unknown representativeness against a system that changes without notice.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
Move 1: Build a longitudinal observatory that repeatedly samples a fixed, segmented query set across major models, then records brand inclusion, framing, factuality, citations, and answer volatility rather than pretending there is a reliable “share of AI voice” metric. What makes this hard is that outputs are stochastic, personalized, model-versioned, and observable only through a biased sample with no impression denominator.
Move 2: Map claims and citations back to likely source ecosystems, then run controlled interventions—updating owned facts, improving machine-readable evidence, and earning independent coverage—to test which sources actually change answers. What makes this hard is that model training and retrieval are opaque, effects have unknown lags, and competitors or model updates can contaminate every test.
Move 3: Turn validated findings into a governance loop that prioritizes consequential misrepresentation, assigns remediation owners, and measures downstream lift through geo, audience, or time-based experiments instead of equating mentions with business value. What makes this hard is that causal business impact may remain unidentifiable without platform logs, while any useful optimization system will invite spam and metric gaming.
answers.first_move: Start by repeatedly measuring a fixed set of real customer questions across the major answer engines.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is separating your intervention’s effect from stochastic outputs, hidden retrieval logic, and continuous model changes.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: 1. Run recurring synthetic prompt batches across the top foundation model APIs to baseline how often, where, and alongside which competitors your brand is cited. The difficulty is that synthetic API calls do not reflect real-user context, chat history, or the bespoke retrieval pipelines deployed in consumer interfaces. 2. Reverse-engineer the citations and domain footprints returned in retrieval-augmented answers to focus digital PR and content distribution solely on the third-party sources the models clearly trust. The difficulty is that you are forced to optimize against opaque third-party consensus and black-box indexers rather than web properties you own. 3. Restructure your own public-facing technical and product information into clean, authoritative, machine-readable formats to maximize extractability during live browsing. The difficulty is that training weights, context window truncation, and model hallucinations mean even perfectly structured facts can be ignored or distorted.
answers.first_move: Run automated query tests across major models to see who they cite instead of you.
answers.hardest_part: You cannot inspect the query volume, user intent, or retrieval pipelines of closed ecosystems.

format.label: Pseudocode
format.instruction: Express the approach as short annotated pseudocode. The comments should carry the reasoning; the code should carry the structure. Around 15 lines.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
```
# 1. Stop trying to measure "rank". There is no SERP. Sample a distribution instead.
prompts = generate_prompt_universe(category, jobs_to_be_done, buying_stage)  # thousands, not dozens
for p in prompts * models * personas * n_trials:      # same prompt, 20x, temp>0 = 20 answers
    a = ask(p)
    log(brand_mentioned, position, sentiment, claims_made, citations_returned)
# Output is a share-of-voice distribution with error bars, not a number. Report the variance;
# the variance IS the finding, and most vendors hide it to look like rank tracking.

# 2. Separate the two causal paths, because they need different fixes.
#    (a) retrieval path: what the model can fetch right now -> fixable via content/citations
#    (b) parametric path: what's baked into weights -> only movable over training cycles
for mention in mentions:
    attribute_to = classify(citations_returned, grounded_or_hallucinated)
# Expect ~half to be unattributable. Say so out loud rather than inventing attribution.

# 3. Influence experiments, not "optimization" best practices.
#    Hypothesis: models cite whoever third parties already frame as the answer.
#    So test earned/aggregator surfaces (reviews, listicles, Reddit, docs, Wikipedia)
#    AGAINST owned-site schema work. My bet: owned-site llms.txt/schema underperforms badly.
run_holdout_experiment(treatment=third_party_corpus_seeding, control=onsite_structured_data)
measure(delta_in_mention_probability, lag_weeks=4..12)  # index/refresh lag is the real cycle time

# 4. Tie to money without pretending you have clickstream.
#    AI referrals underreport; treat it as a dark channel.
model_incrementality(assisted_lift = geo_or_time_based_holdout, not last_click)
```

Where I disagree with the consensus: the industry is racing to build "AI rank trackers" because that's the artifact clients know how to buy. It's the wrong artifact. The answer surface is non-deterministic, personalized, and model-versioned  iction \u2014 a single ranking number is a fabrication with a dashboard around it. The defensible product is a *measurement instrument* that reports distributions and admits uncertainty, plus an experimentation loop. Also: the leverage is almost certainly not on your own website. It's in the corpora models actually trust, which means AEO looks more like PR and community seeding than like technical SEO \u2014 and that is uncomfortable for the people currently selling it.
answers.first_move: Build the prompt-sampling harness and run the same prompts twenty times each to see how unstable the answers actually are before promising anyone a metric.
answers.hardest_part: You are trying to attribute cause in a system where the mechanism is hidden, the output is stochastic, and the model itself changes underneath your experiment \u2014 so a clean before/after can never be distinguished from a silent model update.

format.label: A checklist
format.instruction: Give a checklist someone could actually run next quarter. Each item concrete enough to be marked done or not done. Six items at most.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Six items, runnable next quarter. I'd sequence them measurement-first, and I'd deliberately skip most of what the AEO vendor pitch tells you to do.

1. **Ship server-side AI instrumentation before buying any AEO tool.** Done = your log pipeline separately tags (a) referral sessions from chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai, gemini, copilot, claude.ai and (b) crawler hits from GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, in a table analysts can query. Report crawl and citation as two different things — being crawled is not being cited, and conflating them is the most common self-deception here. Also quantify what you *can't* see: the share of assisted sessions arriving as direct or branded-search with no referrer. If that number is large, say so out loud rather than modelling it away.

2. **Size the actual displacement before funding a program.** Done = a one-page memo with AI-referred sessions as a share of non-brand organic, the trailing 6-month slope, and conversion rate versus organic (in my experience it's a small share of volume with unusually good intent). If it's under ~2% and flat, the honest answer is "instrument and wait," and you should be willing to write that. Deciding in advance what number would make you *not* build a program is the discipline that keeps this from becoming theatre.

3. **Build a prompt panel with error bars, not a rank tracker.** Done = 150–300 prompts derived from real inputs (site search, sales-call transcripts, support tickets, Reddit threads) — not keyword tools — run 5+ times per model per week, logging model version, date, geo, and grounded-vs-parametric answer. You report share-of-voice with a confidence interval and refuse to report week-over-week deltas smaller than the interval. Expect run-to-run variance to swamp most of your "optimisation" wins, and expect a model release to break your time series entirely; note version changes on every chart.

4. **Separate the two problems and only work the tractable one.** Done = each tracked prompt is classified as retrieval-grounded (answer cites live sources) or parametric (answer from weights). Grounded answers are influenceable in weeks; parametric ones move on training-data timescales you don't control. Publish the split. My contrarian view: on-site work is mostly not the lever. Schema, FAQ blocks and llms.txt have no demonstrated effect on citation — llms.txt in particular is a standard nobody enforces. The citations cluster on third-party pages: listicles, Reddit, G2/Capterra, Wikipedia, trade press.

5. **Map and attack the citation corpus, not your own site.** Done = for your top 50 commercial prompts, a ranked list of the domains and specific URLs that actually get cited, with an owner assigned to each of the top 20. Then run real work against it: get into the "best X for Y" listicles you're missing, fix factually wrong claims where you're already cited, correct your Wikipedia article's sourcing, seed genuine practitioner answers in the communities that get quoted. This is digital PR and analyst relations with a retrieval target, and it should probably be staffed from comms, not SEO.

6. **Run one causal test and one accuracy monitor.** Causal test, done = you changed exactly one third-party asset (one listicle inclusion, one Wikipedia fix), pre-registered the affected prompt set plus a matched control set of prompts you didn't touch, and reported the difference in citation share with an interval. This is the closest thing to incrementality available, and it will probably be underpowered — report that honestly rather than claiming a lift. Accuracy monitor, done = a weekly flagged list of false claims about your brand (dead pricing, discontinued SKUs, competitor confusion, invented policies) routed to a named owner with a fix path. This is the deliverable that will actually get executive attention and legal support, and it's the one part of AEO where the value doesn't depend on solving attribution.

What I expect to run into: no denominator for real prompt volume, so share-of-voice is directional forever; personalisation and memory making "the answer" a fiction; vendors selling AI-visibility scores built on synthetic prompt sets that quietly correlate with existing organic rank; and pressure to declare a win from a movement that is inside the noise band. Also worth naming: even if you get cited, the click may never come. Some of this surface is a brand-awareness channel wearing a performance channel's clothes, and measuring it with performance tooling will make it look like a failure.
answers.first_move: Turn on server-log tagging for AI referrers and AI crawlers so we can see what's actually reaching the site today.
answers.hardest_part: There's no observable prompt distribution and no clean counterfactual, so you're trying to prove causal influence over a nondeterministic system whose inputs are mostly pages you don't own.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
- [ ] Define a 100–200 prompt benchmark from real customer jobs, segmented by funnel stage, market, language, and whether naming a brand is appropriate; freeze 80% for quarter-over-quarter tracking and reserve 20% as a holdout.
- [ ] Run the benchmark weekly across the five answer surfaces that matter most, with repeated runs and controlled variants for location, account state, and wording; store complete answers, citations, timestamps, and model/version metadata—not just screenshots or rank.
- [ ] Establish a baseline with uncertainty bands for brand inclusion, recommendation share, factual accuracy, sentiment, citations, and answer volatility; explicitly reject a single “AI visibility score,” because stochastic outputs and prompt selection make it falsely precise.
- [ ] Build a source-influence map by linking claims and citations back to pages, publishers, feeds, reviews, forums, and structured data; manually validate a sample, since citation presence does not prove that a source caused the answer.
- [ ] Ship 3–5 controlled interventions—such as correcting entity data, publishing directly answerable evidence, improving comparison pages, updating partner feeds, or earning independent expert coverage—and preregister the prompts, expected claim change, timing, and untreated comparison set for each.
- [ ] Evaluate changes after recrawl/indexing windows using repeated measurements and downstream signals such as qualified direct traffic, branded search, assisted conversions, and sales-call mentions; document what moved, what did not, and where attribution remains unknowable before scaling any tactic.
answers.first_move: Create a fixed benchmark of real customer questions and capture how major answer engines respond today.
answers.hardest_part: The genuinely hard part is separating causal influence from normal model volatility, hidden retrieval changes, personalization, and correlated publishing across the web.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach:
1. Build a tracked corpus of 50 non-branded, high-intent buyer prompts and run an automated weekly probe across ChatGPT Search, Perplexity, and Gemini to log brand citation frequency and co-occurring competitors.
2. Extract and rank the top 20 external domains cited across those model outputs to map the actual retrieval index instead of guessing search rank.
3. Audit and secure coverage on the top five non-owned consensus sites (e.g., specific Reddit threads, review aggregates, niche trade publications) identified in step 2.
4. Restructure core product documentation and pricing pages into concise, declarative entity-relationship facts to maximize clean extraction by web crawlers.
5. Log referral traffic from AI domain referrers (e.g., perplexity.ai, chatgpt.com) against tracked prompt citation changes over a 12-week test to check for any real attribution link.
answers.first_move: Run 50 buyer questions through ChatGPT and Perplexity to list every website they cite when answering.
answers.hardest_part: LLMs pull from proprietary, dynamic retrieval layers and opaque consensus weights, so you cannot reliably isolate why a model cited your competitor instead of you.

format.label: A lullaby
format.instruction: Write it as a short lullaby: three or four gentle rhyming couplets someone could actually sing. Soft on the surface, honest underneath. The problem is still unsolved when the song ends, and the song should know it.

Hush now, the dashboard is glowing tonight,
